summary: IGMP and MLD are how hosts tell multicast routers which groups they want. This informational RFC offers guidance for tuning IGMPv3 and MLDv2 queries, timers and counters so they work better in mobile and wireless networks.

eli5.summary: When kids keep moving between rooms, the teacher must count more often. This explains how often to call out roll to match.

questions: how to tune igmp for wireless networks
how does multicast work on mobile devices
subtitle: Optimizing multicast group membership protocols for wireless and mobile networks.

tldr.problem: IGMP and MLD protocols work in wireless and mobile networks but waste battery power and spectrum when using default timers. Mobile hosts move frequently, network links are lossy, and bandwidth is limited, making the standard query intervals and robustness settings inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: IGMPv3 and MLDv2 provide configurable parameters—general query interval, query response interval, robustness variable, and others—that can be tuned to the conditions of a specific wireless network. Routers that track membership explicitly can send fewer queries. Shorter startup intervals speed up handover when hosts move.
tldr.outcome: This memo provides guidelines for tuning IGMP/MLDv2 parameters in different mobile network scenarios to balance responsiveness, battery consumption, and link reliability.

today: RFC 6636 is Informational and provides operational guidance for tuning IGMP and MLD in mobile and wireless networks. It does not change the IGMPv3 or MLDv2 protocol specifications, only suggests configuration values for wireless deployments.

sections.title: IGMP and MLD in Wireless Networks
sections.content: The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) for IPv4 and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) for IPv6 let hosts join and leave multicast groups and let routers track group membership. In traditional networks, default timers work fine. But in wireless and mobile networks, these protocols cause problems. Mobile devices run on battery, and wireless links have limited bandwidth and higher packet loss. Hosts move between networks, which can disrupt service setup and teardown. The default general query interval of 125 seconds means that if a host leaves abruptly (powers off, moves away without sending a leave message), the router takes two minutes to notice and stop forwarding multicast to that link. This wastes bandwidth and battery power. Query response timeouts also create bursts of reply traffic that congest limited spectrum. This memo provides tuning recommendations for routers and proxies to optimize IGMP/MLDv3 and MLDv2 behavior in wireless and mobile environments.
sections.eli5: Calling roll every two minutes is normal for a classroom, but if kids are always moving in and out, the teacher might need to call roll more often to keep up.

sections.title: Explicit Membership Tracking
sections.content: A key optimization technique is explicit tracking, where the router keeps a record of which hosts have joined which groups on its downstream interfaces. When a host reports leaving a group (a State-Change Report), the router immediately recognizes that this is the last member and does not need to send group-specific queries to confirm. This reduces the number of reply messages. Without explicit tracking, the router must query to verify the last member has truly left, generating extra traffic. Explicit tracking requires the router to have enough memory and processing power to maintain per-host, per-group state, which is feasible for most access routers but may be challenging for routers with thousands of downstream hosts. This memo recommends enabling explicit tracking on wireless access routers if resources permit, as it significantly reduces multicast signaling overhead in mobile networks.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking everyone 'Who is still interested in reading?' every time, a teacher who remembers who raised their hand can just stop handing out books to those who did not.

sections.title: Tuning Query Intervals and Robustness
sections.content: The general query interval (default 125 seconds) can be adjusted based on wireless link capacity. For routers with explicit tracking on links supporting many hosts (over 200), the memo suggests increasing the interval to 150 seconds to reduce query traffic and conserve battery. For higher-capacity links, a shorter interval of 60 to 90 seconds speeds up membership synchronization. The query response interval (default 10 seconds) controls how long hosts have to reply; longer intervals (10 to 20 seconds) reduce congestion on lossy links but increase join and leave latency, while shorter intervals (5 to 10 seconds) on reliable links provide faster response. The robustness variable (default 2) controls how many times hosts retransmit membership reports; it can be reduced to 1 on reliable links or kept at 2 on lossy links. The last member query timer (LMQT) affects leave latency; with explicit tracking, LMQC can be set to 1 (making LMQT 1 second on stable links) or 2 on lossy links. Startup query interval (normally 1/4 of general query interval) can be shortened to 1 second to speed handover in Mobile IPv6 scenarios.
sections.eli5: If the classroom is stable and quiet, call roll every 2-3 minutes. If kids keep moving in and out, call roll more often. If the classroom is noisy, give kids more time to answer, but accept some might not hear.

sections.title: Mobile IP Network Deployment Scenarios
sections.content: Three deployment scenarios apply IGMP/MLD tuning differently. In direct wireless scenarios, a mobile host connects directly to a wireless access router, and tuning recommendations from Section 3 apply directly. In tunneled scenarios (common in Mobile IPv6), a host sends IGMP/MLD messages through a bidirectional tunnel to a home router. Tunnel conditions are variable and depend on distance; parameters should compensate by increasing query intervals to offset tunnel delay or increasing robustness to offset packet loss. In proxy scenarios (Proxy Mobile IPv6), a foreign router acts as IGMP/MLD proxy, summarizing membership from downstream hosts and sending reports upstream to a home router through a tunnel. Since the number of downstream routers is small compared to hosts, query response intervals can be shorter on the home router. The memo recommends that routers dynamically adjust parameters based on measured round-trip times and packet loss, though it does not specify how to do so.
sections.eli5: Direct connection: tune as suggested. Through a tunnel: account for delay and packet loss. As a proxy: fewer respondents, so can be more aggressive.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security
sections.content: This memo assumes routers and hosts support IGMPv3 or MLDv2 (full or lightweight versions) and does not address backward compatibility with older IGMP/MLD versions. Explicit tracking does not work with older versions due to report suppression, so mixed deployments must avoid explicit tracking. The memo does not introduce new protocol mechanisms or security vulnerabilities; it only suggests tuning of configurable parameters. Operators must ensure that tuning does not break interoperability with hosts or other routers that have not been similarly tuned. Lighter-weight versions like LW-IGMPv3 and LW-MLDv2 are compatible and offer protocol simplicity benefits for mobile implementations.
sections.eli5: These are guidelines, not new rules. Old protocols will not understand the new timers, so mixed deployments need care. Security is the same as with standard IGMP/MLD.
